extracted.intended_audience: stakeholders in immigration rulemaking (immigration attorneys, advocates, affected individuals, regulated parties, and members of the public submitting comments); also DHS adjudicators and policy staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for the proposed rescission of the 2022 Public Charge ground of inadmissibility rule, including (a) the legal/administrative criteria DHS will use for public-charge determinations and (b) instructions and procedural requirements for submitting effective public comments and PRA (information collection) comments on the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors for public charge determinations (INA 212(a)(4)(B)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge, consular officers and immigration officers must, at a minimum, consider the alien's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites INA sec. 212(a)(4)(B)(i). These are mandatory baseline factors; DHS indicates it will continue to treat them as required considerations when making individualized determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support may be considered (INA 212(a)(4)(B)(ii) and sec. 213A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 212(a)(4)(B)(ii) permits the consular or immigration officer to consider any Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA submitted on the alien's behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain aliens (notably most family-based immigrant applicants and many adjustment applicants) must submit a sufficient Affidavit of Support executed by a sponsor who agrees to maintain the sponsored alien at an annual income not less than 125 percent of the Federal poverty line. DHS notes the affidavit is a factor officers may consider in determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances and officer discretion (prospective evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public charge determination is discretionary and prospective: it is made 'in the opinion of' a consular or immigration officer and should be a totality-of-the-circumstances review rather than based on any single dispositive factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM emphasizes reinstating a totality framework (as reflected in pre-2022 guidance and the 2019 Final Rule), and underscores that receipt of public benefits alone should not be sufficient for a finding of inadmissibility. The agency interprets 'in the opinion of' to reflect inherent discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of applicability of public charge ground
rubrics_metrics.description: The public charge ground applies to any alien who applies for a visa, admission, or adjustment of status — including those applying for temporary or permanent visas, admission at ports of entry, and adjustment of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM also notes some categories of aliens are exempt from the public charge ground; those found inadmissible on public-charge grounds may be eligible for waivers or to submit a public-charge bond under INA sec. 213.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions, waivers, and public-charge bonds (INA sec. 213 and related provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some categories of aliens are exempt from the public charge ground; aliens found inadmissible on this ground may apply for a waiver or submit a public charge bond. The Secretary has discretion under INA sec. 213 to admit an alien inadmissible only on public-charge grounds upon the giving of a suitable and proper bond or undertaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM proposes to retain certain public charge bond provisions while rescinding other regulatory provisions; proposed amendments include cancellation and breach rules for bonds (8 CFR 103.6(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of 2022 regulatory definitions and framework (proposed rescission of 8 CFR 212.20–212.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to remove the public charge inadmissibility provisions implemented by the 2022 Final Rule, including removal of definitions and the regulatory framework for making public charge determinations (8 CFR 212.21), removal of the regulations outlining the determination (8 CFR 212.22), removal of exemptions and waivers (8 CFR 212.23), and removal of applicability provisions (8 CFR 212.20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the 2022 Final Rule imposed narrow definitions and limits on factors and benefits considered; rescission is intended to restore broader officer discretion and allow formulation of future policy and interpretive tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of public benefits and resources to be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to remove limitations on the types of public resources relevant to determining whether an alien is dependent, including removing explicit references to 'public cash assistance for income maintenance' and 'long-term institutionalization at government expense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NPRM seeks to move away from a narrow, 'primary dependence' standard and remove regulatory limits on benefit types, allowing consideration of a broader set of resources and benefits under the totality framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future policy guidance to consider mandatory factors, individualized factors, and empirical data
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS intends, after rescission of the 2022 regulations, to formulate policy and interpretive tools that will guide officers to consider: (1) the mandatory statutory factors in section 212(a)(4)(B) of the INA; (2) all individualized case-specific factors and circumstances relevant to an alien's case; and (3) any empirical data relevant to an alien's self-sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit desideratum for future guidance: individualized, fact-specific decisions based on totality of circumstances and available empirical evidence to assess likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory content and format expectations for public comments on the NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that will provide the most assistance should reference a specific portion of the proposed rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that support such recommended change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments must be submitted via http://www.regulations.gov using DHS Docket No. USCIS-2025-0304 and should include the agency name (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) and the docket number. Comments submitted in other ways (emails, letters to DHS/USCIS officials, hand-delivery, courier, or on digital media like CDs/USBs) will not be considered. Comments will be posted without change and may include any personal information provided; DHS may withhold or redact content affecting individual privacy or that is offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and posting rules for comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be submitted in English, or an English translation must be provided. All submissions will be posted, without change, to the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal at http://www.regulations.gov and will include any personal information you provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because submissions are public, commenters are advised to limit personal information. DHS may withhold/redact information it determines may impact privacy or is offensive; see the Privacy and Security Notice at regulations.gov.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information collection (PRA) comment requirements — OMB control numbers and separate deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on information collections described in the Paperwork Reduction Act section must be received by January 20, 2026 and must include the following OMB Control Numbers: Form I-485 (1615-0023), Form I-945 (1615-0143), and Form I-356 (1615-0141).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRA comments are submitted to the same docket as the NPRM but have a different deadline and require explicit identification of the listed OMB control numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPRM comment period deadlines and electronic submission timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Written comments on the NPRM must be submitted on or before December 19, 2025. The electronic Federal Docket Management System will accept comments prior to midnight eastern time at the end of that day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will not accept comments submitted after the deadline via other channels; if unable to use regulations.gov, contact the Regulatory Coordination Division at the provided telephone number for alternate instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docket access and identification requirements for commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: To access the docket, read background documents or comments, and to sign up for alerts, use http://www.regulations.gov referencing DHS Docket No. USCIS-2025-0304.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All comments submitted to the docket are publicly viewable (subject to possible redaction); including the correct docket number and agency name is required for the submission to be associated with this rulemaking.
